analysis.one_liner: Caps executive pay at 100 times a company's average worker pay unless most shareholders approve more.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have limited how much a publicly traded company can pay any one employee: pay could not exceed 100 times the average pay of all the company's employees in a year, unless at least 60% of shareholders voted to allow it [S2] [S3]. Company proxy statements would also have to show the lowest, highest, and average employee pay and how many people earn more than 100 times the average [S3]. It was introduced in May 2009, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary workers at publicly traded companies would have gained a measure of visibility and restraint on executive pay: boards could not pay anyone more than 100 times the average employee without winning 60% of shareholder votes, and shareholders would see exactly how wide the pay gap is at their company [S2] [S3]. Shareholders themselves would gain a mandatory vote on any pay above that cap, giving them real leverage over compensation decisions [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It caps an employee's pay at 100 times the average pay of all employees at the same publicly traded company, unless at least 60% of shareholders vote to approve anything above that.

It requires company proxy materials to disclose the pay of the lowest-paid, highest-paid, and average employee, plus the total amount paid to everyone earning over 100 times the average, making internal pay gaps visible to shareholders.

analysis.who_pays: Highly paid executives and the companies competing for their talent would have borne the cost, since the bill would cap pay or force a supermajority shareholder vote to exceed it [S2]. Companies would also have faced new disclosure requirements in their proxy statements [S3].

drawbacks.text: The 100x cap is a blunt instrument: at a small company with a handful of employees, average pay is high enough that even 100x the average could exceed what many large-company executives make, and the cap applies to any 'employee' of any publicly traded firm, not just top officers.

Even with 60% shareholder approval available as an escape valve, some compensation could simply be restructured through subsidiaries, contractors, or deferred arrangements if the SEC's rules under the bill leave gaps, since the definition of covered compensation depends on future SEC rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but modest: the strongest provision is the disclosure of pay ratios and how many employees exceed 100x the average, which can arm shareholders and the public with information they do not have today [S2] [S3]. The hard cap is far blunter than most pay-reform proposals and could create distortions at very small firms with tiny payrolls, which is the best good-faith objection to it [S2] [S3]. Weighing them, the bill was a targeted response to post-bailout anger over executive pay, but it never received even a committee hearing, so none of its benefits or costs were ever tested in public debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Durbin introduced the bill on May 7, 2009, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.

The Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Christopher Dodd, took no recorded action on the bill — no markup, no hearing, no committee vote — and the Congress ended January 3, 2011, without the bill ever coming to a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public companies and their executives are better off because the bill died: no cap on pay relative to the average worker and no supermajority shareholder vote requirement was ever enacted. Ordinary workers gained nothing.

for.name: Richard J. Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and delivered introductory remarks, but had no cosponsors and could not get it considered in committee.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration, and it stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Financial services industry
against.what_they_did: Financial firms lobbied heavily in 2009-2010 against restrictions on executive compensation and banking regulation as the broader Wall Street reform debate unfolded, though the sources do not connect this lobbying to this specific bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a single Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party, so it never drew a partisan roll call or a clear measure of support.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: The bill would cap any employee's pay at 100 times the company's average unless 60% of shareholders approved more, directly limiting executive pay packages. It never advanced, so no limits took effect.

Shareholders would gain a mandatory vote on any pay above the cap and detailed pay-gap disclosures in proxy materials, giving them more control over compensation decisions. Many shareholders already receive a non-binding 'say on pay' vote under separate law, so the practical gain is incremental.
The bill would add a new SEC rulemaking duty within one year of enactment. It never became law, so no new authority was created.
